title: Collapse in the hallway
scene: An adult collapses in a clear hallway. They do not respond and are only gasping.

steps.why: Gasping is not normal breathing. Get help immediately.

choices: Simulate calling 911, send for an AED and begin CPR following dispatcher guidance.
Wait for the nurse before doing anything.
steps.why: Calling for help and starting CPR must not be delayed. Follow the dispatcher and AED.

title: Lunchroom emergency
scene: A classmate suddenly cannot speak, cough effectively or breathe while eating.

steps.why: Inability to speak or breathe can indicate severe choking.

choices: Simulate calling 911 and get help. Give age-appropriate back blows and thrusts as instructed.
Give water to wash the food down.
Reach into the mouth without seeing an object.
steps.why: Get emergency help promptly; use appropriate choking first aid, never a blind finger sweep.

title: Accident in the workshop
scene: A student has a deep arm wound with heavy, continuous bleeding. The machine is switched off and the area is safe.

steps.why: Heavy ongoing bleeding can be life-threatening.

choices: Simulate calling 911 and apply firm direct pressure with a dressing if safe.
Rinse the wound instead of controlling the bleeding.
Keep lifting the dressing to check every few seconds.
steps.why: Control life-threatening bleeding promptly and use dispatcher guidance.

title: Seizure during class
scene: A student falls and begins jerking. An adult says this is their first known seizure.

choices: Simulate calling 911, clear nearby hazards and get an adult.
Put an object between their teeth.
steps.why: A first known seizure needs emergency help. Protect them from nearby hazards without restraint.

choices: When the seizure started and whether breathing returns to normal.
steps.why: Time the seizure if possible and observe breathing; do not delay getting help.

title: Allergic reaction at lunch
scene: A student develops swollen lips, difficulty breathing and widespread hives after eating. They have their prescribed auto-injector.

steps.why: Breathing trouble with allergy symptoms may be anaphylaxis.

choices: Simulate calling 911 and get help with their prescribed epinephrine following the device and dispatcher instructions.
Wait to see if the symptoms pass.
steps.why: Anaphylaxis can progress rapidly; emergency help and prompt prescribed epinephrine are important.

title: AED has arrived
scene: An adult is unresponsive and not breathing normally. Someone has called emergency services and another person brings an AED.

choices: Turn on the AED and follow its prompts.
Put the AED beside the person and wait.
Wait until the person wakes up.
steps.why: The AED guides the user through its operation. Minimize interruptions to CPR.

steps.prompt: The AED says it is analyzing. What now?
choices: Make sure nobody touches the person while it analyzes and follow its instructions.
Keep a hand on the person to steady them.
steps.why: Stay clear when the device analyzes or delivers a shock, then follow its prompts to resume CPR.

title: Infant choking
scene: A baby is awake but cannot cry, cough effectively or breathe.

steps.why: Infants require a different choking response than older children or adults.

choices: Get emergency help and alternate 5 back blows with 5 chest thrusts as instructed.
Use abdominal thrusts on the baby.
Try to sweep the mouth even if no object is visible.
steps.why: Use infant-specific care, not abdominal thrusts or blind finger sweeps. If the infant becomes unresponsive, start CPR as directed.

title: Hot pan burn
scene: A small area of an adult’s forearm touches a hot pan. They are awake and breathing normally.

steps.prompt: What is the best immediate cooling choice?
steps.why: Cool water helps limit thermal injury. Ice and greasy substances are not appropriate initial care.

steps.prompt: What should you do if a burn is large, deep or involves the face?
choices: Get urgent emergency help as appropriate.
Ignore it because the pain might fade.
steps.why: Serious burns require professional evaluation; do not intentionally break blisters.

title: Unknown medicine
scene: A younger child may have swallowed an unknown amount of medicine. They are awake and breathing normally.

steps.prompt: Who should an adult contact promptly for expert guidance?
choices: A friend who has taken the medicine.
steps.why: Poison Control provides case-specific guidance even before symptoms appear. Call 911 for collapse, seizure, trouble breathing or inability to awaken.

choices: Do not make the child vomit.
Keep the packaging for the adult or specialist.
steps.why: Inducing vomiting can make poisoning worse. Keep information available for the specialist.

title: Sudden changes in speech
scene: An older relative suddenly has a drooping face, weak arm and slurred speech.

choices: Ask them to walk around until it improves.
steps.why: Sudden face, arm or speech changes are stroke warning signs; get emergency help.

choices: When they were last known to be normal.
How many steps they can walk now.
steps.why: The last-known-well time can help clinicians choose treatment. Do not delay transport or give food or drink.

title: Hard collision during a game
scene: A player is dizzy and has a headache after a collision. They are awake, breathing and have no stated emergency danger signs.

choices: Remove them from play and tell the coach or adult.
Ask them to prove they are fine by running.
steps.why: A possible concussion requires immediate removal from play and assessment.

steps.prompt: When may they return to sports?
choices: After appropriate healthcare clearance and a supervised return process.
As soon as the next match starts.
Whenever they say they feel tough enough.
steps.why: Do not return a player with suspected concussion to play that day; follow healthcare guidance.

title: Confusion on a hot field
scene: During outdoor practice, a player becomes very hot and confused.

choices: Wait in the sun until practice ends.
Tell them to run another lap.
steps.why: Confusion with heat exposure is an emergency warning sign.

steps.prompt: While help is coming, what is a priority?
choices: Start rapid cooling safely, with adult help and dispatcher guidance.
Wrap them in a heavy blanket.
Force them to drink while confused.
steps.why: Rapid cooling is important. Do not force fluids on someone who is not fully alert.

title: Injured wrist
scene: A player falls and has a very painful, visibly bent wrist.

choices: Get adult and medical help; keep the wrist supported as found.
steps.why: Do not straighten a suspected fracture. Severe deformity or other danger signs need urgent help.

choices: Numbness, color change or cold fingers.
steps.why: Changes beyond the injury can suggest circulation or nerve problems.

title: Breathing trouble at an event
scene: A participant with asthma is struggling to breathe and cannot speak in full sentences.

choices: Simulate calling 911 and get help for severe breathing difficulty.
Tell them to lie down and wait alone.
steps.why: Severe breathing trouble requires immediate emergency help.

steps.prompt: What is appropriate while help comes?
choices: Help them use their own prescribed rescue medicine as directed, with adult or dispatcher help.
Make them run to clear their lungs.
steps.why: Assist with their prescribed rescue medicine when appropriate; follow their plan and dispatcher guidance.

title: Tick after a hike
scene: After a hike, an adult notices an attached tick on their leg.

steps.why: Remove an attached tick promptly with suitable tweezers.

choices: Grip close to the skin and pull upward steadily.
Coat it with petroleum jelly and wait.
steps.why: Clean the area after removal and seek medical advice for concerning symptoms.

title: Cold and confused
scene: A hiker is wet, very cold, confused and stumbling.

choices: Get emergency help for possible hypothermia.
Tell them to keep hiking alone.
steps.why: Confusion in the cold can indicate dangerous hypothermia.

choices: Move to shelter if safe, handle gently and insulate with dry layers.
Put bare skin against a very hot surface.
steps.why: Prevent further heat loss; avoid rough handling and burns.

title: Danger near the road
scene: You see someone injured beside a road with traffic still moving close to them.

choices: Stay safe and get emergency help from a safe location.
Stand in the traffic lane to film.
steps.why: Do not enter a dangerous scene or become another casualty.

steps.prompt: What should you tell the simulated dispatcher?
choices: Location, hazards, what happened and what you can see.
steps.why: Give a clear location and follow dispatcher instructions.

title: Person struggling in water
scene: Someone is struggling in deep water. You are on shore and have no rescue training.

choices: Call for trained help; reach or throw a flotation aid from a safe position if possible.
Jump in without equipment or training.
steps.why: Avoid becoming another drowning victim. Get rescue help promptly.

steps.prompt: Once trained rescuers bring an unresponsive nonbreathing person to safety, what matters?
choices: Emergency services, CPR including breaths as trained or dispatcher-guided, and an AED.
Wait for them to cough before calling.
Try to drain water by hanging them upside down.
steps.why: Drowning resuscitation needs rapid emergency response and ventilation as well as compressions.

title: Protective gloves
scene: You are selecting supplies for a first-aid kit.

steps.prompt: What helps reduce direct contact with blood?
steps.why: Use gloves if available, without delaying lifesaving care.

title: Identify an AED
scene: A helper asks what equipment to bring for suspected cardiac arrest.

steps.prompt: Which device analyzes heart rhythm and may deliver a shock?
steps.why: An AED provides prompts and can deliver a shock when indicated.

title: Bleeding supplies
scene: You are choosing something to apply direct pressure to a wound.

steps.prompt: Which item is suitable if available?
steps.why: A clean dressing can be used for firm direct pressure.

title: Recognize a tourniquet
scene: You are reviewing bleeding-control equipment with an instructor.

steps.prompt: What is a commercial tourniquet intended for?
choices: Life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg when appropriate.
steps.why: Tourniquets are for appropriate severe limb bleeding. Learn use with certified training and follow dispatcher instructions.

title: Small tools
scene: You are selecting a tool for tick removal practice.

steps.why: Use tweezers to grasp the tick close to the skin.

title: Cold pack
scene: A coach wants to apply a cold pack to a closed injury while arranging appropriate care.

steps.prompt: What should go between the pack and skin?
steps.why: A cloth barrier helps protect the skin.

title: Emergency blanket
scene: You are reviewing a cold-weather kit.

steps.prompt: What is a dry blanket useful for?
steps.why: Insulation helps reduce heat loss; emergency care may still be needed.

title: Time a seizure
scene: A teacher is practicing recording events for responders.

steps.prompt: Which tool helps record elapsed seizure time?
steps.why: Timing helps communicate duration, but never delay care or calling for help to start it.
